messages.subject: Re: rug uses bl default in ggplot but not qplot
messages.subject_clean: rug uses bl default in ggplot but not qplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I think the problem is that geom_histogram() takes 1D input, but by
default, geom_rug() expects 2D input.

The default value of the sides = argument in geom_rug() is "bl", which
means to apply rug plots in both the x- and y-directions. This is a
problem when the only mapped aesthetic is x and the y-value is
derived, in this case from stat_bin() (e.g., ..count.. or
..density..). I found that the following worked:

library(ggplot2)
mydata <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100))
qplot(mydata$x, geom = "histogram" ) + geom_rug()

This is because a histogram layer was produced first, so geom_rug()
would "know" that the y-variable was derived and would adjust
accordingly. OTOH,

qplot(mydata$x, geom = c("histogram", "rug"))

appears to be using x as the input data object for both
geom_histogram() and geom_rug(). There is no problem with the
histogram, since it passes x to stat_bin() to compute the counts, but
geom_rug() appears to be expecting 2D input by default with sides =
"bl" when the actual input is 1D and I think that's responsible for
the error. If we make an adjustment in the qplot() call, it seems to
work:

qplot(mydata$x, geom = c("histogram", "rug"), sides = "b")

You can use geom_rug() with or without sides = "b" and
geom_histogram() in different orders using ggplot() and no error is
thrown.

There are several reasons why I prefer ggplot() to qplot() - I think
you've given me another one to add to the list...

Dennis

Dennis,

Thanks for thoroughly analyzing my code. Your input is very helpful!  I

On 5/30/14, 3:29 38PM, "Dennis Murphy" <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:

>Hi:
>
>You have a few things wrong in your code:
>
>1. The input data frame to ggplot() should be precip, not prec.
>2. Per your code, the object precip$TIMESTAMP is a factor, not a
>POSIXct object, which is what you need to enable date-time formats in
>ggplot2.
>3. In order to use scale_x_datetime(), the scales package must be
>loaded first (as of at least ggplot2-0.9.0, released in 2012).
>
>The first step is to create the proper date-time format in the data
>frame. I do this in two steps because, for some reason, if I compose
>the function calls into one statement, the local time zone is
>retained, which we don't really need here. Add the following lines to
>your code after precip is defined and before invoking ggplot():
>
>library(scales)
>
># Conversions: factor -> character -> POSIXlt
>precip$time <- strptime(as.character(precip$TIMESTAMP),
>                  format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
>
># Convert from POSIXlt to POSIXct
>precip$time <- as.POSIXct(precip$time)
>
>
>As noted by Rajesh, it's also a good idea to add the theme function
>early in the call, so this should get what you wanted:
>
>ggplot(precip, aes(x=time, y=Rain_mm_1_Tot)) +
>  theme_bw() +
>  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +
>  scale_x_datetime(breaks = "1 week", labels = date_format("%D"),
>                   expand = c(0,0)) +
>  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,2)) +
>  labs(title = "Daily Precipitation", x="Date", y="Precipitation (mm)") +
>  facet_grid(source ~ .) +
>  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=60, hjust = 1))
>
>
>However, I'm not a big fan of angled text; I prefer either a different
>presentation format or a coord_flip() when the strings are
>sufficiently long. Here's one alternative date format among several
>that could be applied without string rotation:
>
>ggplot(precip, aes(x=time, y=Rain_mm_1_Tot)) +
>  theme_bw() +
>  geom_bar(stat="identity", position="dodge") +
>  scale_x_datetime(breaks = "1 week", labels = date_format("%b\n%d"),
>                   expand = c(0,0)) +
>  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,2)) +
>  labs(title = "Daily Precipitation", x="Date", y="Precipitation (mm)") +
>  facet_grid(source ~ .)
>
>
>I would be prone to add a line to either the plot title or a figure
>caption to define the range of dates that the graph spans since the
>year is the same in this graph. Alternatively, you could use the
>x-axis label "2014 dates". With multiple year spans, there are other
>ways to format dates.
>
>It's also not clear to me why you need position = "dodge" in
>geom_bar() since you have no grouping factor defined. Taking it out
>produces some warnings about missing values, but I don't see any
>visual difference in the plots with and without position = "dodge"
>(but I could be neglecting something).

messages.body_plain:
In an SQL table I have payments and dates.

I am grouping them into monthly payments and get into a data frame which
looks like

     month   amount
1  2008-02   100.00
2  2008-03   100.00
3  2008-04   250.50
...
13 2009-01   100.00
14 2009-02   125.00
15 2009-03   130.50
16 2009-04   140.00
...
75 2014-05   300.00

I would like to plot the amounts for each month of every year in a
single graph in a different color.

So I reckon I need something like

      2008     2009  2010 ... 2014
01           100.00
02   100.00  125.00
03   100.00  130.50
04   250.00  140.00
...
12

Any pointers on how I do this?

I know that there is no payment for January 2008, so if this an issue, a
pointer on how to add an amount of 0.00 would also be appreciated.

el

ggplot(my.df, aes(x = month, y = amount) + geom_point()

or whatever geom you want to use. It will probably help if you have 'month' in Date form (as.Date(x, format = "%Y-%m)).

Cheers,
Roman

messages.body_plain:
The area under the curves are in fact the same, but those areas are
stacked on top of one another. This makes sense for the default
geom_area, but not for geom_path; when using the path geom you should
also change the position adjustment, e.g.,

ggplot(plotData,
       aes(x = expr, colour = groups)) +
  stat_density(aes(y = ..density..), geom = "path", size = 1, adjust = 0.5) +

  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16))

or take the easy way ant use geom_density() instead of stat_density():

ggplot(plotData,
       aes(x = expr, color = groups)) +
  geom_density(adjust=0.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 16))

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

If you maintain everything else in your code and add position =
"identity" to the stat_density() call, you'll get the same answer as
Ista's. By default, position = "stack" in stat_density(), which
produces the effect that Ista described re area plots - position
"identity" plots the density estimates as is in each group. Even
though the peaks are different in each group, the areas under the
curves are the same - this is visible by noting that the tails of the
'Good' distribution are shorter than those from the 'Poor' one.

Dennis

Hi Vivek
Actually it worked fine although I will sort it in decending order.

The problem was that I use RStudio. which I definately like but once in a long while (maybe one a year?) it goes wonky and that's what it did yesterday.  Just after I replied to us and was ready to shut down for the day I did copy and paste and much to my surprise the paste had the copied text plus about 3 characters from an earlier copy and paste.  A reboot of the computer and reloading of RStudio solved the problem.  Apparently it was not doing the sort you had specified properly.

 For some reason I thought that I had to do the sort with ggplot(), though I cannot remember why I thought that.

Thanks very much for the help.
John
P.S. I hope the baby is sleeping well.

messages.body_plain:
You can accomplish the same without the cast/melt route.

ggplot(mdat, aes(reorder(town, -hours, function(x)x[1]), hours, colour = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_flip()

The idea is to reorder town based on the first element of hours, which will be the hours corresponding to coach1836. I did a quick check and the plot I get resembles the one that Vivek had in his html document.

messages.subject: How to draw this bar plot with precomputed statistics?
messages.subject_clean: How to draw this bar plot with precomputed statistics?
messages.body_plain:
I ran a program and got a count summary. Now I want to generate a figure
like the one produced with the following command:

ggplot(mtcars,aes(factor(cyl))) + geom_bar(aes(fill=factor(vs)),
position="fill")

The only difference between my own data and the above example is that I
got the count summary from another program. It is mentioned in Hadley's
book "ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis" how to display
precomputed statistics, but there is no example in the book. The
description of the section is as below:

"4.9.2 Displaying precomputed statistics
If you have data which has already been summarised, and you just want to
use it, you’ll need to use stat_identity(), which leaves the data
unchanged, and then map the appropriate variables to the appropriate
aesthetics."

I tried without success. Does anyone know how to draw the figure?

My dataset is like this:

 >df <- data.frame(sample=c(rep("case1",3), rep("case2",3),
rep("case3",3)), group=rep(letters[1:3],3), countSum=11:19)

 > df
sample group countSum
1 case1 a 11
2 case1 b 12
3 case1 c 13
4 case2 a 14
5 case2 b 15
6 case2 c 16
7 case3 a 17
8 case3 b 18
9 case3 c 19

The figure I want is like the one produced with the above-mentioned
first command, with "sample" corresponding to "factor(cyl)", "group" to
"factor(vs)", and "countSum" to "count".

Thanks!

Dejian

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, that's a good example that proves this is not a bug, y-axis can differ between rows but be the same within rows under that. Nevertheless, I think this change is unfortunate, since it seems like the entire grammar of facet_grid is then unavailable if your data are not so cooperative.  It would have seemed better to me if the new option were called something like free_y_rows, to indicate that the rows could have their own y's but be consistent across columns, rather than to change the old behavior.

With apologies for not having a more minimal example, consider this data:

writeLines(content(httr::GET("https://github.com/cboettig/sandbox/blob/96c86a5d26bd3eb2c2a35b8a0f92cfde154f257d/example.csv?raw=true")), "example.csv")
dat <- read.csv("example.csv")

ggplot(dat, aes(penalty_fraction, value, fill=penalty_fn, col=penalty_fn))  +
  stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "line") +
  facet_grid(statistic ~ timeseries, scale="free_y")

which creates a graph like this:

which could clearly benefit from some new scales.  I don't see how to construct that without creating each panel separately under this new behavior, which really seems to lose a lot of elegance from the grammar, particularly with large numbers of facets.  While I realize backwards compatibility is not guaranteed, It's also a bit of a shame to realize that figures from some old papers and examples of mine will no longer render correctly.

Any suggestions as to how to work around this most elegantly?

Thanks again for the explanations and the insight so far as well.

Carl

messages.body_plain:
Hi Carl:

There is a fundamental difference between facet_wrap() and facet_grid(): the former facets in one direction and 'wraps' the display in a ribbon-like fashion into multiple rows and columns when the number of levels is sufficiently high, whereas the latter facets by level combinations of two factors. The constraints on facet_grid() are more severe than those on facet_wrap() with respect to scaling.

Your most recent example (BTW, you should have loaded library(httr) before your writeLines() statement since content() is a function from that package) showed that facet_grid() did exactly what it was meant to do: for each level of statistic, you got a different y-scale. Evidently, you want separate y-scales for each panel, but facet_grid() is not equipped to do that, as Kaori noted. If you use scales = "free" in facet_grid(), you'll get the following:

    * separate x-scales in each column of the display;
    * separate y-scales in each row of the display.

It has been this way for some time; I consulted the section of the 0.9.0 transition guide pertaining to facet_grid() and this is the way the scales behaved when scales = "free" was set. When scales are freed in one direction, the above behavior obtains for the free direction and the scaling in the other is fixed.
This is sensible behavior for panels arranged in a grid according to level combinations of two factors.

You can achieve something like what I interpret you want by using facet_wrap() as follows:

ggplot(dat, aes(penalty_fraction, value, fill=penalty_fn, col=penalty_fn))  +
  stat_summary(fun.y = mean, geom = "line") +

  facet_wrap(~ statistic + timeseries, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y")

Unfortunately, the strip panel labeling functions are only available for facet_grid(), so if you don't like the strip labels you'll have to roll your own solution - the simplest is to create an interaction variable in the data and set the factor levels to match the labels you want...but there are other options.

HTH,
Dennis

Well, there's a ">3.2" value in the last row of the ScanRanker_Score
field, which means that variable becomes a factor, which means those
subset statements don't work. If you remove that last row, it'll be
numeric when read in, and then it's easy to do something like this
(note no need to separate out positive and negative values):

ggplot(origdata.long,aes(ScanRanker_Score,value,fill=variable))+geom_bar(stat='identity',position='dodge')

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Cheers,

I am doing a graph that mixeds points and lines together and trying to automate as much as possible. My problem is, when I try to automate it I keep gettin the "Removed 9 rows containing missing values (geom_point)." error message. Generally, the problem with such error is that we try to plot something outside its boundary, but it does not seem to be the case here.

This code works:
names <- c(1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3)
xvals <- c(1:9)
y1vals <- c(1,2,3,10,11,12,15,16,17)
y2vals <- c(2,3,4,11,12,13,16,17,18)
p1vals <- c(1.1,2.1,3.1,11,12,13,14,15,16)
p2vals <- c(0.9,1.9,2.9,10,11,12,13,14,15)

ex_data_p1 <- data.frame(names, long=xvals, lat=p1vals)
ex_data_p1$names <- factor(ex_data_p1$names)
ex_data_p2 <- data.frame(names, long=xvals, lat=p2vals)
ex_data_p2$names <- factor(ex_data_p2$names)
ex_data_l1 <- data.frame(names, long=xvals, lat=y1vals)
ex_data_l1$names <- factor(ex_data_l1$names)
ex_data_l2 <- data.frame(names, long=xvals, lat=y2vals)
ex_data_l2$names <- factor(ex_data_l2$names)

ggplot() +
    geom_path(data=ex_data_l1, aes(x=long, y=lat, group=names, shape='a', linetype='a', colour='a')) +
    geom_path(data=ex_data_l2, aes(x=long, y=lat, group=names, shape='b', linetype='b', colour='b')) +

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

When you create each subplot for lines and points, ggplot2 appears to
be retaining only the last level created. If you plot graph before
adding the manual scales, you'll see that only two levels show up in
the legend, b (from lines) and d (from points).

In the first graph, you created a factor for shape, color and linetype
on the fly by including them within aes() and then used a vector of
breaks containing the generated factor levels in each manual scale
call to inform the scales of the (generated) levels.

In the second attempt where you are pulling in separate lists of data
frames, it appears that your attempt to generate factor levels on the
fly doesn't work when trying to 'add' to the existing ggplot object
graph. The failure likely has to do with how ggplot2 trains the scales
for graph, but I don't know how it works well enough to articulate
what is going on.

One workaround is to create separate data frames for the data that
produces lines and the data that produces points, and to define a
factor with levels a-d in each, even though the
values in one will be a-b and in the other, c-d. You can then create
separate layers for the
lines and points and add the scale modifications at the end.

This doesn't quite match your first graph, but it will give you the
general idea - I'll let you figure out where I messed up. Starting
with

my.lines <- list('a'=ex_data_l1, 'b'=ex_data_l2)
my.points <- list('c'=ex_data_p1, 'd'=ex_data_p2)
my.breaks <- c(names(my.lines), names(my.points))

library(plyr)
# Create data frames by row binding the data frames
# in the two lists - it creates a new variable .id with the
# names of the list components as values/levels
DFlines <- ldply(my.lines, rbind)
DFpts <- ldply(my.points, rbind)

# Make sure that the factor .id has the same levels in each
DFlines[[".id"]] <- factor(DFlines[[".id"]], levels = my.breaks)
DFpts[[".id"]] <- factor(DFpts[[".id"]], levels = my.breaks)

# Plot
ggplot(DFlines, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = names, shape = .id,
                    linetype = .id, color = .id)) +
    geom_path() +
    geom_point(data = DFpts) +
    scale_color_manual('Legend', values=rainbow(4)) +
    scale_shape_manual('Legend', values=c(NA, NA, 19, 19)) +
    scale_linetype_manual('Legend', values=c(1, 1, 0, 0))

I suspect that you have a broader application where the data is split
up into list components and you hoped that you could add to a ggplot
object, but I believe that if you are going to create a factor on the
fly in ggplot(), you have to do it in a single call, not a sequence of
calls. Somewhere ggplot2 has to 'know' the levels of its factors or it
can't train the legends properly. This is why I created separate data
frames for lines and points and then defined .id to have the same
levels in both data frames prior to the ggplot() call. The behavior
you experienced is an indication that ggplot2 could not train the
scales reasonably based on your inputs and reconciled the conflict by
chucking the points.

HTH,
Dennis

I second the reply to check out GGally.  Here is some code and output using GGally to maybe help out. A starting point to get more of what you want is to edit the upper = list(continuous = "density", combo = "box") argument.

Code snippet is below and link to gist is included at end of reply. The output from print(myPairs) looks useful to understanding the data set. This isn't validated and might only meet part of your requirements.

See link below to a .png of the plot output.

I took some liberties and removed missing values.

#install.packages("GGally")
require(GGally)
delme2 <- subset(delme[, c("km3int", "BBndvi2", "SIPI", "PRI570", "TO", "DCNI1")])
delme2 <- na.omit(delme2)
summary(delme2[1:10,])
head(delme2)
myPairs <- ggpairs(delme2[, 1:6],
    upper = list(continuous = "density", combo = "box"),
    lower = list(continuous = "points", combo = "dot"),
    color = "km3int",
    axisLabels = "show",
    title="Example Matrix for Exploration of delme Dataset")
print(myPairs)

messages.body_plain:
Ben is right about needing to remove the > character in your data in record 80. There might be a reason why it's indicated with greater than...maybe an outlier or something else.  Just removing the  > is kind of a hack but gets you on track. :-)

I don't know the data set but it looks like count data. If so, another point is that this is really a histogram but uses geom_bar() geometry.

Also, the melt() will change your subject to a factor so you don't need the line.  Snippet that will work for you:

require(reshape2)
# Must remove ">" character in row 80, then load
origData <- read.table("~/Downloads/scanranker.txt",header=T,sep="")
origDataMelted <- melt(origdata, id.vars=c("subject", "ScanRanker_Score"))
# Counts by x are already summarized, so using geom_bar and not geom_histogram.
# This is Ben's ggplot() call...
myPlot1 <- ggplot(origDataMelted, aes(x=ScanRanker_Score, y=value, fill=variable)) +
    geom_bar(position="Dodge", stat="identity") +
    ylab("count") +
    ggtitle("Histogram of ScanRanker Counts by Each of the Two Variables")
print(myPlot1)

-Phil

Thanks a lot, Dennis.

You have guessed  right. I have different data sets for highways, power lines, railroads, etc. (geom_path) as well as powerplants, reservoirs, etc. (geom_point) that I would like to plot in a map.

Would this behaviour ("it appears that your attempt to generate factor levels on the fly doesn't work when trying to 'add' to the existing ggplot object grap") be considered as me trying to use ggplot2 beyond its boudaries or for something it was not initially conceived?

You "messed up" (if you can call it that, you have been really helpful!) in the fact that the "group=names" argument in geom_path is there to help the function differenciate between different polygons. As such, when merging 'a' and 'b' you are keeping the name '1' for both datasets, and telling the function to draw them as a single polygon which results in such weird behaviour of the red line. This could be avoided when merging the datasets by using 1a for 'a' and 1b for 'b' as group identifiers.

Here are  the lines I have modified on your example to make it fit 100% my initial plot:
ex_data_p1 <- data.frame(names=paste0(names, "p1"), long=xvals, lat=p1vals)
ex_data_p1$names <- factor(ex_data_p1$names)
ex_data_p2 <- data.frame(names=paste0(names, "p2"), long=xvals, lat=p2vals)
ex_data_p2$names <- factor(ex_data_p2$names)
ex_data_l1 <- data.frame(names=paste0(names, "l1"), long=xvals, lat=y1vals)
ex_data_l1$names <- factor(ex_data_l1$names)
ex_data_l2 <- data.frame(names=paste0(names, "l2"), long=xvals, lat=y2vals)
ex_data_l2$names <- factor(ex_data_l2$names)

Again, thanks a lot.

Guillermo

> Hi:
>
> When you create each subplot for lines and points, ggplot2 appears to
> be retaining only the last level created. If you plot graph before
> adding the manual scales, you'll see that only two levels show up in
> the legend, b (from lines) and d (from points).
>
> In the first graph, you created a factor for shape, color and linetype
> on the fly by including them within aes() and then used a vector of
> breaks containing the generated factor levels in each manual scale
> call to inform the scales of the (generated) levels.
>
> In the second attempt where you are pulling in separate lists of data
> frames, it appears that your attempt to generate factor levels on the
> fly doesn't work when trying to 'add' to the existing ggplot object
> graph. The failure likely has to do with how ggplot2 trains the scales
> for graph, but I don't know how it works well enough to articulate
> what is going on.
>
> One workaround is to create separate data frames for the data that
> produces lines and the data that produces points, and to define a
> factor with levels a-d in each, even though the
> values in one will be a-b and in the other, c-d. You can then create
> separate layers for the
> lines and points and add the scale modifications at the end.
>
> This doesn't quite match your first graph, but it will give you the
> general idea - I'll let you figure out where I messed up. Starting
> with
>
> my.lines <- list('a'=ex_data_l1, 'b'=ex_data_l2)
> my.points <- list('c'=ex_data_p1, 'd'=ex_data_p2)
> my.breaks <- c(names(my.lines), names(my.points))
>
> library(plyr)
> # Create data frames by row binding the data frames
> # in the two lists - it creates a new variable .id with the
> # names of the list components as values/levels
> DFlines <- ldply(my.lines, rbind)
> DFpts <- ldply(my.points, rbind)
>
> # Make sure that the factor .id has the same levels in each
> DFlines[[".id"]] <- factor(DFlines[[".id"]], levels = my.breaks)
> DFpts[[".id"]] <- factor(DFpts[[".id"]], levels = my.breaks)
>
> # Plot
> ggplot(DFlines, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = names, shape = .id,
>                     linetype = .id, color = .id)) +
>     geom_path() +
>     geom_point(data = DFpts) +
>     scale_color_manual('Legend', values=rainbow(4)) +
>     scale_shape_manual('Legend', values=c(NA, NA, 19, 19)) +
>     scale_linetype_manual('Legend', values=c(1, 1, 0, 0))
>
> I suspect that you have a broader application where the data is split
> up into list components and you hoped that you could add to a ggplot
> object, but I believe that if you are going to create a factor on the
> fly in ggplot(), you have to do it in a single call, not a sequence of
> calls. Somewhere ggplot2 has to 'know' the levels of its factors or it
> can't train the legends properly. This is why I created separate data
> frames for lines and points and then defined .id to have the same
> levels in both data frames prior to the ggplot() call. The behavior
> you experienced is an indication that ggplot2 could not train the
> scales reasonably based on your inputs and reconciled the conflict by
> chucking the points.

    median.thickness <- 0.25

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Sean, tick marks on log scales are sometimes too sparsely by default.

A few months ago, I wrote a function to address this:

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

enhanced_log_breaks <- function(n = 5, base = 10) {
  function(x) {
    rng <- log(range(x, na.rm = TRUE), base = base)
    if (diff(rng) > 2.5) {
      log_breaks(n = n, base = base)(x)
    } else  if (diff(rng) > 1.5) {
      result <- log_breaks(n = n, base = base)(x)
      sort(c(result, result * 2, result * 5))
    } else  if (diff(rng) > 1) {
      result <- log_breaks(n = n, base = base)(x)
      sort(c(result, result * 0.25, result * 0.5))
    } else {
      result <- pretty_breaks(n = n)(x)
      result[result != 0]
    }
  }
}

# tick marks computed by above function
qplot(x = 1:25, y = cumprod(rep(1.02, 25))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = enhanced_log_breaks())
qplot(x = 1:25, y = cumprod(rep(1.1, 25))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = enhanced_log_breaks())
qplot(x = 1:100, y = cumprod(rep(1.1, 100))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = enhanced_log_breaks())

# ggplot's default tick marks
qplot(x = 1:25, y = cumprod(rep(1.02, 25))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = log_breaks())
qplot(x = 1:25, y = cumprod(rep(1.1, 25))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = log_breaks())
qplot(x = 1:100, y = cumprod(rep(1.1, 100))) + scale_y_log10(breaks = log_breaks())

Hope this helps,
Lukas

messages.body_plain:
Lily,

You want to make a distinction between what as.Date stores and what you want to see printed out. You can format the output from as.Date using format()  to include very simple or very complicated date expressions which are in character form.

scale_x_date can also be configured for special formats. But when you define a character value as.Date you want to give it the Year, month and day as a basic identifier.

HTH

David

Hi:

The lack of response to your question is a function of its ambiguity
as well as a lack of a reproducible example. A noted in another reply,
the date format you want in a plot does not have to be the same as the
date format in the data. If you frame your question more concretely
and provide a minimal reproducible example, you'll get a more accurate
and more expeditious reply.

You can see some examples of date formats here:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

See section 7.1 and pay attention to the labels argument in the examples.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: about setting date
messages.subject_clean: about setting date
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This is a fairly simple solution to your immediate problem:

DF <- read.table(header = TRUE, text = "

year  month  moist
2003  01       53.7875
2003  02       55.9037
2003  03       65.9075

2003  04       71.9154")

# Create a variable with a Date format - I arbitrarily set the
# day of the month to be the 1st
DF$date <- with(DF, as.Date(paste(year, month, "01", sep = "-")))

# Once you have a variable of class Date, you can use the function
# scale_x_date() to format the date axis; the date_format() function
# below comes from the scales package, so it needs to be loaded
# (and installed)

library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Two different ways to format the date axis
ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = moist)) +
   geom_line() + geom_point() +
   scale_x_date(breaks = DF$date, labels = date_format("%Y-%m"))

ggplot(DF, aes(x = date, y = moist)) +
   geom_line() + geom_point() +
   scale_x_date(breaks = DF$date, labels = date_format("%b\n%Y"))

The possible formats you can use are listed in ?strptime.

More inline....

> One input example is file='worldmap.Rdata', how to convert a vector or
> raster file to this .Rdata file?

A .Rdata file is an R binary file. You load it into a session with

load("myfile.Rdata")

To use geom_map() in ggplot2, the input file to the function must be a
data frame.
See http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/fortify.sp.html if the file is of
a class generated
by the sp package - that shows you how to convert a spatial data set to a data
frame readable by ggplot2.

If your input file is of some class not associated with the sp package, you'll
have to do some web searching unless some kind soul provides the links to you.
There is information on the web pertaining to plotting maps of various
formats in
ggplot2, but I'm not aware of any document or web site that has put it
all together.

You might also want to look into the ggmap package, which provides more
flexibility in map formats than does ggplot2 but uses ggplot2 to
produce the graphics.
See http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-1/kahle-wickham.pdf for
an overview of
the package's capabilities.

Dennis

I don't know the function well enough to explain the behaviour but am replying with a tip that is helpful in situations like this. I'm also adding an example.

messages.subject: RE: qplot boxplot and ylim
messages.subject_clean: qplot boxplot and ylim
messages.body_plain:
If you want to set up a common display scale, make sure that the limit covers the range of possible data in each panel.

If you use limits, and if there is data point(s) outside the range of the limits, those data points are dropped.

In your example data,

y <- c(3,2.3,3.1,16,16.5,20)
16, 16.5, 20 are dropped if you set up ylim=c(0,8)

This is equivalent to:

qplot(x,y,data=d,geom="boxplot") + scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,8))

If you don’t want to drop the data but just zoom in the area, use coord_carterian instead (see the difference in output).

qplot(x,y,data=d,geom="boxplot") + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,8))

messages.body_plain:
On 6/16/2014 6:34 AM, Torben Tvedebrink wrote:
> How can I parse the context of a grouping/colour variable to the guide?
> I.e. I would like to use the following syntax:
> ggplot(data,aes(x=x,y=y)) + geom_line(aes(colour=guide))
> where the variable 'guide' is a part of the data.frame 'data' and contains
> strings like "q[1] == 0.03" and so on.
> Is there a parse=TRUE option somewhere for guides() or the like?

There is not a parse option for guide labels, but you can get the same
effect with a custom label function

First some dummy data

DF <- data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10,
                  guide=rep(c("q[1] == 0.03", "q[2] == 0.45"), each=5))

Now the custom label function

guideparse <- function(x) parse(text=x)

And an example in use

ggplot(DF, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
   geom_line(aes(colour=guide)) +
   scale_colour_discrete(labels=guideparse)

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

  geom_point() +
  xlab("label") +
  ylab("label on\ntwo lines") +
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,1,2.0), "cm"))

  geom_point() +
  xlab("label") +
  ylab("label on\nthree\nlines") +
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,1,1.55), "cm"))
p2
ggsave("plot-1.png", plot=p1, scale=0.8)
ggsave("plot-2.png", plot=p2, scale=0.8)

messages.subject: Re: how to make the shape thicker in the scatterplot
messages.subject_clean: how to make the shape thicker in the scatterplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Thankfully, this thread was resurrected so I'll give it a shot. This
should get you close to what you want. Using a simple toy example,

DF <- data.frame(x = rnorm(30), y = rnorm(30),
                 gp = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 30, replace = TRUE))

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

p <- ggplot(DF, aes(x, y)) +
       geom_point(aes(shape = gp, fill = gp), size = 3.5,
                  color = "black") +
       scale_shape_manual(values = 21:25)

grid.edit("geom_point.points", grep = TRUE, gp = gpar(lwd = 2))

Notes:

1. Shapes 21-25 allow fill color, which explains the choice in
scale_shape_manual().
2. To thicken the line borders, you need to use grid graphics
directly. This is what the last line does, which comes from a
StackOverflow question answered by Sandy Muspratt in August, 2013:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/17677687/change-thickness-of-a-marker-in-ggplot2
3. You need to fix the point color before you can thicken the shape
borders; clearly, you want the border color to differ from the fill
color unless you want to play with alpha transparency, which is
another option..
4. I know the next question is going to be how to make the border
thickness in the legend the same as that in the graph. I tried without
success. It probably involves some combination of guide_legend() with
the override.aes argument and some appropriate incantation from grid
graphics, but I don't know enough about the latter yet to make it
work. Perhaps someone else can fill the gap.

Dennis

Hi:

Making the logical leap that Col.D is supposed to represent a mean and
Col.E a standard deviation/standard error, here's a way to do it:

# It's better to use dput() to send data by e-mail than copy/paste
from the terminal.

d <- structure(list(Col.A = structure(c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 1L,
1L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L,
3L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("Type.A", "Type.B", "Type.C"
), class = "factor"), Col.B = structure(c(1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L,
2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L,
2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L, 1L, 2L), .Label = c("gene1", "KDM5B"
), class = "factor"), Col.C = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L,
5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L), Col.D = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1.4, 0.9,
1.2, 0.7, 1.5, 1.4, 2.5, 1.3, 2.1, 0.8, 2.4, 2.2, 5.1, 1.5, 4.4,
0.85, 4.7, 4.5, 10.2, 2.6, 8.9, 1.5, 11.2, 10.8), Col.E = c(0,
0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.14, 0.08, 0.11, 0.05, 0.17, 0.13, 0.22, 0.1,
0.19, 0.06, 0.23, 0.18, 0.4, 0.12, 0.34, 0.08, 0.37, 0.25, 1.2,
0.2, 0.6, 0.13, 1.2, 1.1)), .Names = c("Col.A", "Col.B", "Col.C",
"Col.D", "Col.E"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c("1", "3",
"4", "6", "7", "9", "10", "12", "13", "15", "16", "18", "19",
"21", "22", "24", "25", "27", "28", "30", "31", "33", "34", "36",
"37", "39", "40", "42", "43", "45"))

# Using ggplot() instead of qplot():

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(d, aes(x = Col.C, y = Col.D, color = Col.B)) +
   geom_line() +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Col.D - Col.E, ymax = Col.D + Col.E),
                  width = 0.3) +
   facet_grid(Col.A ~ .)

# qplot():
qplot(Col.C, Col.D, data = d, color = Col.B, geom = "line") +
   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Col.D - Col.E, ymax = Col.D + Col.E),
                  width = 0.3) +
   facet_grid(Col.A ~ .)'

If my interpretations of Col.D and Col.E are incorrect, it's your
responsibility to clarify what means what in this data set.

Dennis

messages.subject_clean: setting minimum value for displaying bins in geom_hex and geom_bin2d
messages.body_plain:
I have plotted some data using geom_hex and geom_bin2d, which are fantastic. In short, I am plotting the locations, by depth and latitude, at which fishing vessels deployed fishing gear.

Unfortunately I cannot publically display bins that contain values less than 3 because of legal reasons.

I have tried the following to mask the bins with less than 3 records:

1) using scale_fill_continuous to set the low value color to white, yet this masks more bins than necessary

2) using scale_fill_continuous to limit the values to those greater than 3, yet this appears to turn those cells with fewer than 3 records to a dark gray (which makes them even more visible).

3) using scale_fill_discrete, which produces an error.

I see that geom_bin2d has a drop argument for zero values. I'm after the same functionality but I want to drop cells where the count is less than 3.

I believe I could use the hexbin package to eliminate cells with fewer than 3 records yet I'd prefer to find a solution in ggplot2.

I'm relatively inexperienced in R and ggplot2, so apologies if this question is vague. Suggestions would be very much appreciated. My code is pasted below. I could not easily figure out how to generate a fake dataset to simulate the same circumstances.

lat.depth <- ggplot(data, aes(y = AVG_LAT, x = AVG_DEPTH,)

lat.depth + geom_hex(bins = 20) +

   scale_fill_continuous(limits = c(3, 500))

messages.subject: Re: boxplot + jitter
messages.subject_clean: boxplot + jitter
messages.body_plain:
Here's a toy example to illustrate how you could do something like this. The key is to break the data up into two data frames, one of which is used to produce the boxplots in one layer and the other to produce the jittered stripplots in a second layer. Also notice that the levels of the grouping factor are the same in both data frames.

DF1 <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], each = 50),
                              levels = LETTERS[1:4]),
                   y = rnorm(100))

DF2 <- data.frame(gp = factor(rep(LETTERS[3:4], each = 5),
                              levels = LETTERS[1:4]),
                   y = rnorm(10))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF1, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_point(data = DF2, position = position_jitter(width = 0.3))

An alternative is to use geom_dotplot() in place of geom_point():

ggplot(DF1, aes(x = gp, y = y)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_dotplot(data = DF2)

Dennis

Hi,

I have been making some line graphs in ggplot2 using geom_line() .   In this example, I have been using a user-defined palette.        My data is in long-form, and has the following variables: (value, event, ids, rank).  I am plotting on the x-axis the event (1 to 10) and on the y-axis the value.  Each separate line is a different id (ids variable).   There are 18 ids, A->R.     Each id is given a rank of 1-18 based on their value at the final timepoint (event=10).

James Curley

  geom_line(lwd = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = getPalette(colourCount)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values=c(5,5,4,6,6,2,5,1,2,4,4,3,3,6,1,2,3,1)) +

messages.body_plain:
Here's a solution, but if anyone understands why my first attempt
(using stat='identity', see below) doesn't work, I'd appreciate
knowing. Anyway, hope this works for you.

library(ggplot2)
library(hexbin)
df <- data.frame(x=runif(1000),y=runif(1000))  # sample data

# pre-summarise the data
hexinfo <- hexbin(df$x,df$y,xbins=10)
df_hex <- data.frame(x=hexinfo@xcm,y=hexinfo@ycm,count=hexinfo@count)

# suppress too-small values and plot
ggplot(subset(df_hex,count>3),aes(x,y,fill=count))+geom_hex(stat="identity")

# I don't understand why this doesn't work. The hexagons are actually being
# plotted (try color='red' to see them) but are very tiny; something about the
# scale is screwed up. geom_hex bug? My mistake?

# Different approach - map hex cell counts back to original data
hexinfo <- hexbin(df$x,df$y,xbins=10,IDs=TRUE)
df$cell <- hexinfo@cID
df$hexcount <- hexinfo@count[df$cell]

ggplot(subset(df,hexcount>2),aes(x,y))+geom_hex()  # compare these two plots
ggplot(subset(df,hexcount>4),aes(x,y))+geom_hex()

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Removing NA from stacked distribution bargraphs
messages.body_plain:
I would suggest that the missing data is informative and your graph is better as is since there is an increasing trend in missing responses over time, but if you really want yearly sums of 1, I'd suggest removing the NAs in the data before passing it to ggplot(); e.g.,

ds1 <- subset(ds, !is.na <http://is.na>(attend))
ggplot(ds1, ...) + ...

or

ggplot(subset(ds, !is.na <http://is.na>(attend)), ...) + ...

BTW, as an exercise, try this in the R console:

ds <- read.table(header = TRUE, text = "
<copy/paste the data from your message here>
")

and see what happens. This is why copy/paste from the console is not helpful to those who are trying to help you. See ?dput and Google "R reproducible example" for better ways to send data via e-mail to text-oriented mailing lists.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: setting minimum value for displaying bins in geom_hex and geom_bin2d
messages.subject_clean: setting minimum value for displaying bins in geom_hex and geom_bin2d
messages.body_plain:
See inline in several places.

On 6/21/2014 3:11 AM, Ben Bond-Lamberty wrote:
> Here's a solution, but if anyone understands why my first attempt
> (using stat='identity', see below) doesn't work, I'd appreciate
> knowing. Anyway, hope this works for you.
>
> library(ggplot2)
> library(hexbin)
> df <- data.frame(x=runif(1000),y=runif(1000))  # sample data
>
> # pre-summarise the data
> hexinfo <- hexbin(df$x,df$y,xbins=10)
> df_hex <- data.frame(x=hexinfo@xcm,y=hexinfo@ycm,count=hexinfo@count)
>
> # suppress too-small values and plot
> ggplot(subset(df_hex,count>3),aes(x,y,fill=count))+geom_hex(stat="identity")
>
> # I don't understand why this doesn't work. The hexagons are actually being
> # plotted (try color='red' to see them) but are very tiny; something about the
> # scale is screwed up. geom_hex bug? My mistake?

The problem here is how you extract the x/y coefficients of the hexagons
from hexinfo. xcm and ycm are the center-of-mass of the data in the
hexagon, not the center of the hexagon. Thus those points are not on a
hexagonal grid. When geom_hex goes to plot them, it determines what size
hex grid will put those points on in a regular hexagonal grid. It is a
fine grid that will do that. Here is the proper way to extract the
center of the hexagons for ggplot to use:

df_hex2 <- data.frame(hcell2xy(hexinfo), count=hexinfo@count)

# now this works

ggplot(df_hex2,aes(x,y,fill=count)) +
   geom_hex(stat="identity") +

> # Different approach - map hex cell counts back to original data
> hexinfo <- hexbin(df$x,df$y,xbins=10,IDs=TRUE)
> df$cell <- hexinfo@cID
> df$hexcount <- hexinfo@count[df$cell]
>
> ggplot(subset(df,hexcount>2),aes(x,y))+geom_hex()  # compare these two plots
> ggplot(subset(df,hexcount>4),aes(x,y))+geom_hex()
>
> Ben
>

> On Fri, Jun 20, 2014 at 1:05 AM, Corey N <nilescbn-Re5JQE...@public.gmane.org> wrote:
>> I have plotted some data using geom_hex and geom_bin2d, which are fantastic.
>> In short, I am plotting the locations, by depth and latitude, at which
>> fishing vessels deployed fishing gear.
>>
>> Unfortunately I cannot publically display bins that contain values less than
>> 3 because of legal reasons.
>>
>> I have tried the following to mask the bins with less than 3 records:
>>
>> 1) using scale_fill_continuous to set the low value color to white, yet this
>> masks more bins than necessary

You could use scale_fill_gradientn to make everything below 3 the same
color (setting breaks a 0, 3, and whatever the max is and mapping those
points to the colors white, white, and blue(?)). However, see the next
point for a better alternative.

>> 2) using scale_fill_continuous to limit the values to those greater than 3,
>> yet this appears to turn those cells with fewer than 3 records to a dark
>> gray (which makes them even more visible).

This is the right approach, but with one additional step: set the
missing value to clear.

   scale_fill_continuous(lim=c(3,17), na.value=NA)

Unfortunately, if you set the lower limit, you have to also set the
upper limit; there is no way to say to set it to whatever it would have
been.

>> 3) using scale_fill_discrete, which produces an error.

Right. Because it is continuous.

>> I see that geom_bin2d has a drop argument for zero values. I'm after the
>> same functionality but I want to drop cells where the count is less than 3.
>>
>> I believe I could use the hexbin package to eliminate cells with fewer than
>> 3 records yet I'd prefer to find a solution in ggplot2.
>>
>> I'm relatively inexperienced in R and ggplot2, so apologies if this question
>> is vague. Suggestions would be very much appreciated. My code is pasted
>> below. I could not easily figure out how to generate a fake dataset to
>> simulate the same circumstances.
>>
>>
>>
>> lat.depth <- ggplot(data, aes(y = AVG_LAT, x = AVG_DEPTH,)
>>
>> lat.depth + geom_hex(bins = 20) +
>>
>>     scale_fill_continuous(limits = c(3, 500))
>>

Here is an example using all the approaches:

library("ggplot2")
library("hexbin")
set.seed(123)
# sample data, following Ben
df <- data.frame(x=runif(1000),y=runif(1000))

# The basic plot, using just ggplot. Setting the sizes using binwidth
# rather than bins because it will be easier this way to match
# the other approaches.
# Adding a text annotation so that we can verify exactly what is in
# each hex. Also setting coord_equal since this example is a square
# grid and this will keep proportions the same. Both of these are
# there for showing what is going on (and making sure that the right
# thing is happening) and would not (necessarily) be part of the
# final plot.

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = ..count..)) +
   geom_hex(bins=10) +
   geom_text(aes(label=..count..), stat="binhex", binwidth=c(0.1,0.1),
             colour="white") +
   coord_equal()

# pre-summarise the data
hexinfo <- hexbin(df$x, df$y, xbins=10, xbnds=c(0,1), ybnds=c(0,1))
# Extract the _centers_ of the hexagons as the x and y coordinates
df_hex <- data.frame(hcell2xy(hexinfo), count=hexinfo@count)

# This is identical to the previous plot; Before using this technique
# to subset, I want to make sure I can reproduce without the subset.
ggplot(df_hex,aes(x,y,fill=count)) +
   geom_hex(stat="identity") +
   geom_text(aes(label=count), colour="white") +
   coord_equal()

# suppress too-small values and plot
ggplot(subset(df_hex,count>3),aes(x,y,fill=count)) +

   geom_hex(stat="identity") +
   geom_text(aes(label=count), colour="white") +
   coord_equal()

# However, we do not need to pre-summarize the data. Use the
# scale to enforce the limit. The downside to this is that
# the upper limit must also be specified (manually). Note
# setting na.value in addition to setting the limits.
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = ..count..)) +
   geom_hex(bins=10) +
   geom_text(aes(label=..count..), stat="binhex", binwidth=c(0.1,0.1),
             colour="white") +
   scale_fill_continuous(lim=c(3,17), na.value=NA) +
   coord_equal()

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Manual color and linetype, and additional geom with fixed color
messages.subject_clean: Manual color and linetype, and additional geom with fixed color
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have many lines in one plot and to differentiate between them I want to combine color and linetype following the suggestion here:
http://stackoverflow.com/a/11344735/1463740

This works fine. However, I want to add another geom with a fixed color. This color overwrites all other colors, but only when using the combination of color and linetype as described above. Here is an example:

#############################

library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)

d <- data.frame(x=c(rep(1,10), rep(2,10)),
                y=c(seq(1,10), seq(2,11)),
                model=letters[seq(1, 10)])

p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, color=model)) + geom_line()
p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, color=model, linetype=model)) + geom_line() +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(rep("solid", 5), rep("dashed", 5))) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(brewer.pal(5, "Paired"), brewer.pal(5, "Paired")))

## similar colors
p1
## works as expected but similar colors
p1 + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, colour="black", geom="line")

## easier to distinguish
p2
## all elements black
p2 + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, colour="black", geom="line")

#############################

Is this a bug or a feature? What can I do?

Thanks a lot!
Sebastian

Subject: create ggplot2 graphics in Java using R

Hello,

I have create a desktop application in Java using Swing. I would like to generate a heatmap graphic to show it in my app as an image so I installed rJAva and through JRI it connects to R.

I wrote my R script in R for generating and saving to hard disk my ggplot2 heatmap graphic. So far so good, Java connects with R perfectly in the java side. In hte other side, R creates the image perfectly in Rstudio.

The problem exists when I connect from Java (through rJAva/JRI libraries) to R, to generate the ggplot2 graphics. It only generates a blank png. If it were a plot graphic instead of a ggplot2 graphic it wouldn´t have any problem.

My Java code which connects to R:

File mapa = new File("D:\\trading_tools\\javaBBB\\BBBproject\\files\\mapas\\cosa.png");

if(!mapa.exists()){

    Rengine re=new Rengine (new String []{"--vanilla"}, false, null);

    if (!re.waitForR())  {

        System.out.println ("Cannot load R");

        return;

    }

    writeCSV(); //function which wrotes 'test2csv.csv' in hard disk

    re.eval("require(ggplot2);require(XML);require(rjson)");

    re.eval("csv<-read.csv('D:/trading_tools/javaBBB/BBBproject/files/mapas/test2csv.csv',head=T,sep=';',dec='.',colClasses=rep('numeric', 24))");

    re.eval("png(filename='D:/trading_tools/javaBBB/BBBproject/files/mapas/cosa.png', width = 400, height = 400)");

    re.eval("g<-ggplot(csv[1:nrow(csv),], aes(x=sl,y=tp)) + geom_tile(aes(fill=CA))");

    re.eval("dev.off()");

    re.end();

}

I read in some webs that ggplot2 doesn´t generate the graphics out of R.

Can sombebody help me please? Any workaround or different option?

I thought about converting the project in a web application and then use Rserve but I am afraid of doing all the work to finally have the same issue in Rserve.

Does anybody have experience in this issue?

Any suggestion or help will be appreciatted!

Thanks in advance and best regards.

--

I would consider that a bug. Fortunately it's easy to work around:

ggplot(d, aes(x=x, y=y, color=model, linetype=model)) +

    stat_summary(fun.y=mean, color="black", geom="line") +

    geom_line() +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(rep("solid", 5), rep("dashed", 5))) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(brewer.pal(5, "Paired"),
brewer.pal(5, "Paired")))

Note that the order matters--geom_line() has to come after stat_summary().

Best,
Ista

messages.subject_clean: Manual color and linetype, and additional geom with fixed color
messages.body_plain:
I take it back, the only bug was in my brain, probably due to
insufficient coffee. The issue is simply that stat_summay is creating
separate lines for each model, because of the linetype mapping. You
can make it create only a single line by overriding the group mapping,
like this:

p2 + stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun.y=mean, colour="black", geom="line")

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: heat map on Scatter plot
messages.subject_clean: heat map on Scatter plot
messages.body_plain:
Try using geom_tile().

You're right that stat_density2d() will color by count.

Here is an example. Shading is based on the value of the Volume measure as you need:

require(ggplot2)
# experiment using 10 to show that shade is on value, not on count.
measure <- c(sample.int <http://sample.int>(10, size=1000, replace=TRUE))
x <- sample(LETTERS[3:12], 1000, replace=TRUE)
y <- sample(LETTERS[3:12], 1000, replace=TRUE)
DF <- as.data.frame(cbind(x, y, measure), row.names=FALSE)
DF$measure <- as.integer(DF$measure) # to control the data type
names(DF) <- c("dim1", "dim2", "Volume")
str(DF)
myPlot <- ggplot(DF, aes(x=dim1, y=dim2, fill=DF$Volume))
myPlot <- myPlot + geom_tile()
myPlot <- myPlot + scale_fill_gradient(low="yellow", high="red")
myPlot  # there are different ways to build and print the plot, this is just one way.
rm(myPlot)  # destroy object each time prior to trying different options

This is crude and the list of variations are numerous. It should get you going.

-Phil

On 6/26/2014 7:26 AM, Woody Setzer wrote:
> I am plotting count data that is strongly skewed, but include 0's, so I
> want to use a square root scale on x and y so the small values are not so
> crowded together. I would like a tick at 0 to make it clear where the
> bottom of the range is, but scale_x_sqrt refuses to plot one for me. Here
> is an example set of code:
>
>    ## Construct the test data set
>    x <- rlnorm(30)
>    x <- (x - min(x)) / max(x) * 700
>    y <- rlnorm(30)
>    y <- (y - min(y)) / max(y) * 700
>    tdta <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)
>
>    ## Plot it naively, accepting defaults:
>    p <- ggplot(data=tdta, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + scale_x_sqrt() +
> scale_y_sqrt()
>    print(p)
>    ## No tick at 0, just at 200, 400, 600.
>
> ## If I explicitly add breaks, there is no change.
>    p <- ggplot(data=tdta, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() +
>      scale_x_sqrt(breaks=c(0,200,400,600)) +
>      scale_y_sqrt(breaks=c(0,200,400,600))
>    print(p)
>
> How can I get a tick-mark at 0?

Short answer:

You need to add an expand=c(0,0) argument to both the scale_x_sqrt and
scale_y_sqrt calls.

Long answer:

This was tricky. My first few (standard) answers for this (use
expand_limits(x=0, y=0) or setting the limits in the scale call) didn't
work. I decided it has to do with the scale sqrt transformation because
it worked fine with aes(x=sqrt(x), y=sqrt(y)).

By this point, I was using a different test data set:

tdta <- data.frame(x = seq(0,2,by=0.1),
                    y = seq(0,2,by=0.1))

I finally figured out that what was happening was that when the scale
was expanded (by default, the scale is expanded by 5% of the range in
each direction to give some padding between the extreme data/labels and
the edge of the plot), this was giving a negative number which was then
being inverted back to a positive number (greater than 0) which then put
the 0 break outside the limits.

library("scales")
# specifying limits of 0 to 2
sqrt(c(0,2))
expand_range(sqrt(c(0,2)), 0.05, 0)
# new limits after expanding and transforming back; now excludes 0
expand_range(sqrt(c(0,2)), 0.05, 0)^2

In the transformed space, negative numbers have no meaning and they
should not be being mapped to just their square. Mapping them all to
zero solves this problem, but requires creating a new transformation.

library("scales")
mysqrt_trans <- function() {
   trans_new("mysqrt",
             transform = base::sqrt,
             inverse = function(x) ifelse(x<0, 0, x^2),
             domain = c(0, Inf))
}

Then you can specify this transformation be used with

ggplot(data=tdta, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
   geom_point() +

   scale_x_continuous(trans="mysqrt") +
   scale_y_continuous(trans="mysqrt")

which gives a nicer looking graph with the expected padding and breaks
and 0 shows up as a break.

> Thanks!
>
> Woody Setzer

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

On 6/26/2014 8:36 AM, Brandon Hurr wrote:
> No idea how but I'll add that the smallest whole number it will accept is 2
> and I've got it down to 1.674027. I think it may relate to the padding that
> ggplot adds to the edges of a plot. You get too close and you're in
> negative numbers which only my imaginary friends can understand.
>
> That's my hypothesis anyway.

You were right. It was interaction between the padding (expand argument)
and the scale transformation.

As to why 1.674027, it depends on the range of the original data (which
can differ since the data was randomly generated). In the example given,
the upper bound can't be more than 700. Were it 700, the derivation goes

limits in data scale: 0, 700
limits in transformed scale: 0, 26.457 (square root of 0, 700)
expanded limits in transformed scale: -1.32287, 27.78038 (extending by
5% of the range each way)
expanded limits in data scale: 1.75, 771.75 (squaring previous numbers)

So any breaks less than 1.75 are "outside" the limits and so aren't drawn.

(I have a workaround in a separate answer, but thought you might be
interested as to why such an odd number was the limit).

messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/2014 9:59 AM, Woody Setzer wrote:

> Woody Setzer

I'm not sure about that either. I _think_ that it only goes through the
last inverting process prior to break determination, which then leaves
some breaks out. But that deciding what data points to include or
exclude happens on the transformed scale (where 0 is above the negative
lower bound) and so the points at 0 are still displayed. That was one of
the aspects that was confusing me, too.

I am writing up a bug report about it now.

>>> is an example set of code:

>>>     p <- ggplot(data=tdta, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + scale_x_sqrt() +
>>> scale_y_sqrt()
>>>     print(p)
>>>     ## No tick at 0, just at 200, 400, 600.
>>>
>>> ## If I explicitly add breaks, there is no change.

>>>       scale_x_sqrt(breaks=c(0,200,400,600)) +

  Probably the best way to do this is
colour=interaction(Treatment,Timepoint) [you may want to create the
interaction up front, as a new variable in your data set, rather than on
the fly].

  It gets tricky if you want the colours to be related (e.g. red vs blue
for two times, light vs dark for two treatments) -- using
colour=Timepoint, alpha=Treatment can work, or you can make the
interaction and set up scale_colour_manual however you like.
